#1059. Germany's women: Ena Mahmutovic makes her case to become Germany's next No.1 goalkeeper

Germany's win against Australia saw Ena Mahmutovic excel in goal. The 22-year-old Bayern Munich goalkeeper is considered the successor to Ann-Katrin Berger and is making a name for herself.

With determination, pace, and four beautifully crafted goals, Germany's women won its friendly against Australia, thrilling not only the fans but also head coach Christian Wück.

"You can see how fired up the girls are, how well they're already playing together, and that we have an incredible amount of talent on the field and on the bench," said a delighted Wück after his team's well-deserved 4-2 victory.

Since there were several notable absences, including captain Giulia Gwinn and top scorer Lea Schüller, others had to step up and fill the gaps. And they did so with flying colors. Melissa Kössler made a strong case for herself as a striker by scoring her first two international goals. Center back Camilla Küver and Sjoeke Nüsken were also on the scoresheet.

Much like it was with the men's team during Jürgen Klopp's first international break as Germany head coach, the question as to who will emerge as the next number one goalkeeper for the women was also a hot topic.

The difference is that unlike Manuel Neuer, who has retired from international football, Ann-Katrin Berger is sticking around for at least one more tournament cycle.

However, with just three matches to go before the start of the playoffs in the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL), where she plays for Gotham FC, Berger is giving these two Germany friendlies a miss.

This means 22-year-old Bayern Munich goalkeeper Ena Mahmutovic, who is seen as a potential successor to Berger, took her her chance.

"Ena deserves to play the next match," Wück said ahead of the game. "We must not forget that she already kept a clean sheet in Slovenia (Germany's last World Cup qualifier). And I hope she can repeat that tomorrow."

Some will draw parallels to Jonas Urbig, who many see as a future number one for Germany's men. Both he and Mahmutovic were born in 2003 in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, and both are seen as up-and-coming stars for their club and country.

The difference is that while Urbig remains an understudy to Neuer at Bayern, Mahmutovic is already the first-choice keeper at her club, having won the starting job over Maria Luisa Grohs prior to the start of the season.

For Germany, though, Mahmutovic still has to bide her time, while there are already strong indications that Klopp intends to make Urbig his number one.

"I'm obviously delighted," Mahmutovic said ahead of the games.

"It's always something special, of course – especially playing against a team from another continent. I think testing ourselves against them is very helpful as we look ahead to the World Cup."

Bayern director Bianca Rech recently described Mahmutovic as "the future of the national team," calling on Wück not only to give her a callup, but also regular playing time.

Wück still sees Berger as slightly better than Mahmutovic, but he is also full of praise for the young keeper.

"Ena's performances have been very good," he said. "She will get her playing time."

The match against Slovenia was just Mahmutovic's second appearances for Germany. Her first, which came almost two years ago, was memorable for the wrong reason. In the dying minutes of a friendly in December 2024, she lost control of the ball after a back pass, allowing an Italian forward to score the winner in a 2-1 defeat for Germany. Still, Mahmutovic was included in Germany's squad for the 2025 Euros.

Had it been up to her father – who is from Montenegro – Mahmutovic would never have become a goalkeeper.

"He still says I would have been better as an outfield player because I'm good with both feet," she said.

That's a quality that evidently wasn't lost on Thomas Gerstner, when her coach at her then-club Duisburg, gave her her Women's Bundesliga debut in May 2020. With the team coping with several absences, the then-16-year-old, who had been on the bench as backup goalkeeper, came on as an outfield player.

"The coach brought me on during stoppage time," Mahmutovic recalled. "I got to make two sprints – that was my debut."

That, however, was a one-off, and nobody questions Mahmutovic's strengths as a goalkeeper.

"She is one of the most talented goalkeepers in the world," said Bayern coach Jose Barcala, noting that she is the kind of player who can decide a match.

Mahmutovic will be hoping she gets many more opportunities to do just that for Germany.

This article was originally published in German.

This article was updated on October 12 after Germany's friendly against Australia.

#1057. The brain liquidates billions of mutant neurons around the time we’re born

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

By the time a baby is born, its brain has lost large numbers of neurons with genetic abnormalities.Credit: Getty

Around the time of birth, the developing human brain mysteriously tidies up by purging itself of a vast number of mutation-riddled neurons, according to a painstaking analysis of more than 2,300 nerve cells.

We are all mosaics: vast genetic diversity found between cells in a single person

We are all mosaics: vast genetic diversity found between cells in a single person

The analysis, published in Nature1 on 28 October, found that more than one-quarter of the sampled neurons from the brains of human fetuses had either gained or lost several segments of their chromosomes. By contrast, only about 6% of neurons from the brains of babies after birth had such abnormalities. “It suggests that the neurons that survive may be the ones that have kept the most intact genomes during development,” says Christos Proukakis, a neurologist at University College London, who was not involved in the study.

The findings reveal a new mechanism for regulating how many neurons a person has and for deciding which fetal neurons are allowed to persist in the brain, says Diane Shao, a paediatric neurogeneticist at Boston Children’s Hospital in Massachusetts and first author on the paper.

Learning more about this process could be key to understanding neurological conditions that often appear in childhood, such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and epilepsy.

Studies in mice2 have suggested that, during early development, mammals eliminate many brain cells by activating a molecular programme that leads to the cells’ deaths. Shao and her colleagues analysed human brain development by studying the brains of deceased individuals ranging from fetuses at 14 weeks of gestation to nonagenarians. The team focused on neurons in the cerebral cortex, a region of the brain responsible for memory, learning and consciousness, among other functions.

How to make a brain: new experiments challenge existing picture

How to make a brain: new experiments challenge existing picture

The team analysed the genomes of individual neurons to look for those that had either lost or gained some chromosomal segments, a phenomenon called copy number variation. The analysis revealed that a stunning number of cells with widespread copy number variation were present during fetal development. There were so many that Shao and her colleagues spent years trying to work out whether the results were real. But even after repeating the experiment using a different single-cell sequencing method, the results were similar.

After birth, however, the proportion of these abnormal neurons dropped by more than fourfold, suggesting that they had been culled during development.

How does the brain know which neurons are normal and which are not? One possible clue, says Shao, is that those brain cells with high levels of copy number variation also tended to show abnormal activity of genes involved in forming connections, or synapses, with other neurons.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03444-x

Shao, D. D. et al. Nature https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11190-3 (2026).

#1056. Ole Gunnar Solskjaer open to Man Utd return as pressure piles on Michael Carrick

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Carrick’s future as Man United manager is in real doubt with the club hovering above the relegation zone

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Ole Gunnar Solskjaer has suggested that he would be open to a return as Manchester United manager after admitting he has “something unresolved” at the club.

It comes as pressure piles on current head coach Michael Carrick after Saturday’s 2-0 defeat to Chelsea, which left United hovering above the Premier League relegation zone on goal difference.

Carrick’s future was in serious peril last week as United’s hierarchy met at Carrington to discuss next steps, but the decision was made to keep the former Red Devils midfielder in charge for the trip to Stamford Bridge. He is not expected to be sacked before Tuesday’s Champions League meeting with Roma.

But with Carrick seemingly requiring an almighty turnaround to stay in the Old Trafford dugout, former boss Solskjaer has expressed a cautious interest in retaking the reins at United, having been pipped to the position of Ruben Amorim’s successor after interviewing for the interim role earlier in the year.

“Going back to what has been is not always as good,” he told Norwegian outlet TV2.

“Yes, I had lined up [as Manchester United's interim manager after Amorim’s sacking], but I didn't think it would last longer than the summer. It was probably time for someone else to try.

“I also feel like I have something unresolved. Of course it would have been nice to have the opportunity again.”

The Norwegian’s three-year stint between 2018 and 2021 mirrored Carrick’s path at United, brought in as an interim manager before impressing enough to earn a permanent contract, only for performances to dip again after that initial honeymoon period.

Solsjkaer also had Carrick in his backroom staff during his reign, with Carrick then becoming United’s caretaker manager for three games at the tail-end of 2021 after Solskjaer’s dismissal.

Solsjkaer added that he was not intending to oust his former colleague from the United hot seat, stressing that his aforementioned desired return could come after a long and fruitful tenure for Carrick.

“If Michael does well for 10 years and decides to quit, and they ask me if I can take them for two months, of course I wouldn't say no,” he said. “I've been at that club for 18-19 years, so it's part of the family. But it's not something I'm thinking about.

“Michael has what it takes to take that club forward. I think he's the right man. He understands the club, understands the fans and knows what's needed.”

#1055. Dominik Szoboszlai says Liverpool need to dive to win penalties after controversial Isak incident

Alexander Isak had his shirt pulled in the box by Jurrien Timber during Arsenal’s 1-0 win but was denied a penalty and Szoboszlai has suggested Liverpool may have to dive to win spot-kicks

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Dominik Szoboszlai said Liverpool might need to dive to get a penalty in the future after Alexander Isak was denied a spot-kick when he stayed on his feet against Arsenal.

Striker Isak had his shirt tugged by defender Jurrien Timber in Arsenal’s 1-0 win on Sunday but referee Andy Madley did not give Liverpool the decision.

Vice-captain Szoboszlai believes Liverpool players do not normally go to ground but thinks they may have to resort to more dramatic reactions to persuade officials to intervene.

“It’s a penalty,” he said. “I don’t know what they expect from us: to dive or something. I don’t think we are the type of team or players to do that but from now on we might need to do it. If Alex falls down it’s a clear penalty. Timber doesn’t really care about the ball and maybe if he doesn’t pull Alex’s shirt Alex can head it in the goal.”

Szoboszlai feels Liverpool are not the most streetwise of teams, adding: “It is not our type of play. I don’t think in this moment you can think this way that: ‘Oh, let me wait for someone touching me and I’ll fall down’.

“No, he is focusing on the ball and he wants to head the ball in the net. But if you interfere with your hand on his back then he might not do it, then you take a chance from his point of view and it’s a penalty.”

Szoboszlai made his return from a hamstring injury as a replacement and admitted he rushed his comeback earlier when he started against Brentford but came off after half an hour.

“The last three seasons I want to play every 90 minutes but sometimes your body says ‘rest a little bit’ and my body told me to ‘stay calm, you’ve had enough games now’,” he explained.

“I missed games against [Manchester] City and LASK and then I felt again very good after a couple of days off but it seemed I wasn’t ready but sometimes it is my heart and I listen to my heart and not my body. #1053. Aston Villa ‘withdraw threat of legal action’ against Jamie Carragher

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Villa threatened Carragher with legal action after he suggested manager Unai Emery should consider taking the Manchester United job

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Aston Villa have reportedly withdrawn their threat of legal action against Jamie Carragher over comments he made about the club, its supporters and manager Unai Emery.

The row centres on remarks the former Liverpool defender delivered on the Stick to Football podcast last week, where the prospect of Emery replacing Michael Carrick at Old Trafford was under discussion.

Carragher had suggested Emery should consider taking the Manchester United job, arguing that “Aston Villa will never be Man United” in the context of football’s hierarchy, and told Villa fans to “shut the f*** up” if they took issue with that statement.

Villa issued their response on Friday evening, posting a statement on X that was signed by chairman Nassef Sawiris.

“Aston Villa will initiate legal action against Jamie Carragher for his unacceptable insults about the club and its fans,” the statement said.

“Aston Villa will not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football. Nassef Sawiris, Chairman.”

Carragher went on to apologise for his comments on Saturday ahead of Villa’s clash with Fulham, posting on X: “I’d like to apologise to Aston Villa, the owners and their fans. My language this week was clumsy and wrong.

“I can assure Villa fans it was tongue in cheek but I can understand it’s not come across that way, so apologies. Good luck today UTV [Up The Villa]!”

And while Villa never initiated legal action against Carragher, BBC Sport claim that they have now dropped any threat to do so following his apology.

The Independent has contacted Aston Villa for comment.

Emery has overseen a resurgence at Villa since arriving in 2022, lifting them from regular relegation scrappers to Champions League qualification for the first time in over 40 years, before last season guiding them to the Europa League title.

Carragher nevertheless claimed that Emery would jump ship from Villa Park if the opportunity arose to manager a “giant” club again, with the Spaniard previously managing Paris Saint-Germain and Arsenal.

"There is a chain in football, whether you like it or not," said Carragher.

"So Real Madrid will take Manchester United's best player, they did it with [Cristiano] Ronaldo. And there will be teams below Aston Villa, and they'll take their players or manager.

"Aston Villa will never be Manchester United."

#1051. Suzuki howler costs Aston Villa crucial points

Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki went from being serenaded with a chorus of “world’s No 1” to making a bizarre blunder that denied Unai Emery’s side a third successive Premier League victory.

The Villa manager, however, preferred to focus on a string of important saves from Suzuki rather than the uncharacteristic mistake that allowed Fulham to collect a deserved point.

It all went wrong for the hosts just after the hour mark in a match where Fulham provided more than a few scares before finding the net in unexpected fashion.

Alex Iwobi, who had been denied superbly by a Suzuki save just moments earlier, swung in a corner. It was right on top of the Villa goalkeeper, who tried to keep it out but only succeeded in fumbling it over the line. A frantic attempt to gather the ball was in vain and goal-line technology confirmed the goal stood.

Zion Suzuki drops Alex Iwobi's corner and Fulham are level! 🫨 https://t.co/KwLFMRpKqk

Suzuki appeared to have been put off by the presence of Fulham’s Shea Charles, but Emery refused to single out the player for criticism.

“I prefer to speak about the saves that he made,” the Villa manager said. “This is part of football. I think he played fantastically and he is doing a lot of saves so he can make one mistake. It is part of football. We can be mature about this.

“I still want to see consistency. Over the last five Premier League matches, we are winning three and drawing two. It’s not bad but with our poor start it’s not enough.

“We have to change our mind quickly for Tuesday against Barcelona. We want to test ourselves at this level.”

Villa go to the Nou Camp with a 100 per cent Champions League record to their name this season. But they will need to improve on Saturday evening’s performance to get a result in Spain.

As well as Suzuki’s error, a 14th-minute penalty miss from John McGinn also proved costly.

It was awarded after Leon Goretzka, making his full league debut for Villa, saw his header hit Sander Berge’s raised hand. Nobody appealed at the time but referee Sam Barrott was sent to the touchline monitor by VAR to review the incident and gave the spot-kick.

McGinn’s attempt, however, hit the crossbar and the chance to take an early lead went begging. The Villa captain seemed a strange choice to take the spot-kick as he has only ever scored one career penalty, but Emery defended the choice, saying: “We analysed the penalty takers in the squad and it was McGinn here.”

Penalty MISSED! John McGinn hits the bar 💥 https://t.co/2kBYkYA2BY

Nicolas Jackson was on hand to ease Villa’s nerves before the break, though. the Villa manager had said before the game that the striker’s goalscoring capability meant he was capable of matching the likes of Harry Kane. His assessment was backed up by Jackson scoring the opening goal, after 40 minutes, which summed up the striker in one moment of pure power combined with agility.

Collecting Johan Manzambi’s superbly weighted pass, Jackson forced his way past two defenders before sliding in the goal that put Villa ahead.

Emery’s touchline celebrations said it all as the Senegal forward continues to flourish under the man who knew how to get the best out of him at Villarreal.

Nicolas Jackson scores his fifth league goal in five games! 🔥 https://t.co/W0xmFtW1Gt

Suzuki has also flourished under Emery and he kept Villa in the game with some superb saves.

When Antonee Robinson crossed for Gonzalo Garcia, his step over allowed Oscar Bobb in for what looked like his second goal in successive games. But Suzuki pulled off a stunning fingertip save. That had Villa supporters singing: “Zion Suzuki, the world’s No 1”.

Robinson put in another cross and Suzuki got a touch that was enough to make Garcia put his shot wide. Villa were living dangerously and the Japanese goalkeeper made another outstanding stop to keep out Iwobi’s header. But then it all went wrong for Suzuki when he fumbled Iwobi’s corner.

That allowed Fulham’s recent revival under manager, Alvaro Arbeloa, to continue – they now have seven points from their past three games.

“We spoke at half-time about what we had to do,” Arbeloa said. “If you want to win a game you have to fight and I think we have to believe in our way, we’ve shown we can beat anyone in the way that we play but we have to be aggressive.

“We created so many chances and at the end it’s one point in a difficult stadium. I’m so happy with the second half because of the way we played, this is the team that we want to be.”

"This is the first time I've seen him that little bit confused" Rob Green analyses Zion Suzuki's error that lead to Fulham's equaliser 🔍 https://t.co/B3HCivNpwz

"I don't think he gets the flowers he deserves" 💐 Jamie Redknapp is a fan of Calvin Bassey 🫡 https://t.co/R9uravAzRU

“We started the game well. Fulham are a good side, not easy to win [against] but we came in front. We did well but in the second half we gave them more time on the ball. They have good players and they can make chances. We were unlucky with the goal but we tried to keep fighting. It is important not to lose these games.”

On Zion Suzuki’s mistake for Fulham’s equaliser:

“It is frustrating because we do not want to concede goals but it can happen to everyone. Zion is a great guy, great goalkeeper. He will learn from it. We will support him and go again.”

Chance for Aston Villa. Cash clips in a delivery from the right and Torres has a good chance from eight yards out but the Spaniard’s header goes wide.

Changes for both sides. For Aston Villa, they bring Barkley on for Kamara.

Cairney has not been on the pitch long but he is already into the book for cynically bringing down Mbaye.

Fulham are carving Aston Villa open. Bobb drives down their right wing before cutting inside. As he approaches the Aston Villa penalty area, he plays it out to his left to pick out Iwobi in space. Iwobi could hit it first time but instead cuts back onto his right, which allows Cash to block the shot but it does spin behind for a corner.

Before that is taken, Cairney replaces Iwobi. The corner comes to nothing.

Fulham have not made any substitutions yet but based on the way they are playing, they really do not need to right now, unless anyone is exhausted.

You can hear the groans inside Villa Park as the home fans grow frustrated with their side’s performance since the break.

Unai Emery has unsurprisingly made a triple change as Mbaye, Buendia and Gomes come on.

The Aston Villa goalkeeper has been outstanding tonight but that is a huge error. The corner is swung in by Iwobi from the left and Suzuki should simply catch it. He backpedals towards his own line and ends up dropping it. By the time he re-gathers, the ball has crossed the line and Fulham have an equaliser that they deserve.

Zion Suzuki drops Alex Iwobi's corner and Fulham are level! 🫨 https://t.co/KwLFMRpKqk

Another save from Suzuki and Fulham spurn yet more great chances. Bobb’s cross from the right side of the box falls right on the head of Iwobi, who should score, but his header is straight at Suzuki. Garcia then has a shot blocked that goes behind for a corner.

Fulham once more come agonisingly close to an equaliser. Castange flicks on with his head at the near post from a corner out on the left. Charles then flicks it towards goal but it hits his teammate Garcia and loops over the bar. Alvaro Arbeloa will be wondering how his side are behind in this game.

Fulham have started this half positively and have a corner out on the left. They take it short before Iwobi clips it in but the delivery is poor and easily cleared by Goretzka.

How have Fulham not scored there and got back on level terms? Robinson and Iwobi exchange a neat one-two on the left side of the box before the former sends in a dangerous cross. He scored two against Manchester City a week ago and he now has one tonight. He is found in space on the left by Manzambi and drives into the Fulham penalty area. Garcia shoots from the left edge of the box and tries to catch Suzuki out at his near post. Garcia though drags his effort into the side netting as he goes in search of his second Premier League goal.

The Premier League has just posted this on X about the Aston Villa penalty:

VAR: “That’s the hand right up and it hits it”.  AVAR: “For me, his hand is in an unnatural position above his head”.  REF: “After review, Fulham No.16 commits a handball offence with a hand high above the head. The final decision will be penalty kick”.

Berge is pretty close to Goretzka but there is no reason why his arm is above his head like that.

It is adjudged to have been a handball from Berge and Aston Villa are awarded the penalty. That feels like the only decision the referee could come to in all honesty.

Another McGinn corner from the right is met by Goretzka. This time, the German gets his header on target but it is easily saved by his compatriot Leno.

There is a VAR check for a possible penalty. Is there a handball from Berge in there immediately after Goretzka got his head on the ball? It appears that it did strike Berge’s hand and the referee is sent to the screen. We know how this normally goes...

Alysson goes down inside the Fulham box, wanting a penalty, but he is not going to get that.

Aston Villa do have a corner though, which McGinn delivers. His corner is met by Goretzka, who cannot keep his header down and it goes off target.

That is a big early chance for Fulham which Iwobi wastes. Bobb steals possession deep inside his own half and drives forward into the Aston Villa half. He then finds Garcia to his right, who delivers a cross from the right side of the box. There is a nick off Lindelof and comes to Iwobi near the penalty spot but he blazes his effort into the stands. At the very least, Iwobi should be hitting the target.

Is that an example of the time of the game contributing to a decision? Goretzka is pulled back by Garcia, who avoids a yellow card. Had that not been inside the first few minutes of the game, it would not have been a surprise to have seen a yellow card.

With this being Aston Villa’s last home league game before Remembrance Sunday, Villa Park pauses to pay tribute to remember the fallen. Wreaths are laid in the middle of the centre circle before The Last Post is played.

#1050. Pope lung nodule: Could it be cancer?

The case of Pope Leo shows how small lung nodules are often found during routine health checks. Quick treatment is generally advised before nodules can grow to become larger life-threatening masses.

It often takes a chest X-ray or CT scan to spot small lung (or pulmonary) nodules, especially when a patient is asymptomatic.

At less than 3 centimeters (1.1 inches), lung nodules are less likely to press against your airway and cause any chest pain or shortness of breath or wheezing.

In the case of Pope Leo XIV, who told a gathering at the Vatican on October 11, 2026, doctors had found a nodule on his lung, it is unclear exactly how large that nodule is.

All we know (at time of writing on October 12, 2026) is that it was "detected at a very early stage," and that it was "well localized."

That suggests it has not spread or metastasized, although its full status is not publicly known. Doctors advised the pontiff to have his lung nodule removed.

Whether his was a chance finding — or whether the pope had presented with symptoms — we do not know.

But "incidental findings of lung nodule(s) in asymptomatic individuals" is considered an "increasingly common clinical dilemma," according to a 2019 paper published in the Annals of Thoracic Medicine.

This "dilemma" rests in part on the fact that biopsies — removing a small sample of tissue from the spot or nodule to determine whether it's malignant (cancerous) — are difficult to perform on small nodules.

The risks involved in a surgical diagnosis are considered "excessive compared to the relatively low prevalence of malignancy in the small nodules."

That's according to a 2017 paper published in the European Respiratory Review. And that may also be the dilemma that Pope Leo's doctors have faced.

Fortunately many — if not most — early-stage lung nodules are benign. It is also possible to have more than one nodule at a time, and they can all be benign.

It's said the pope will need a week to recover after his operation to remove the lung nodule. He is due to travel to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru between November 6-17.

Lung nodules are generally defined as a white spot or lesion on the lung. They have a rounded or irregular shape.

Radiologists refer to their "opacity" because, compared to the surrounding air-filled lung tissue, lung nodules appear as white or gray spots on a CT scan — that is, they have a certain density.

Lung nodules can be caused by old lung infections, foreign particles that are inhaled and get lodged in the lung, inflammation, scar tissue and indeed the onset of cancer.

At more than 3 centimeters, the nodule is defined as a mass. The bigger it gets, the greater the chance that it will obstruct your airway and the lung's ability to function.

Symptoms may start with chest pain, shortness of breath and wheezing. They may then progress to a chronic cough or coughing up of blood, fatigue, hoarseness, loss of appetite, unexplained weight loss and recurring respiratory infections like bronchitis or pneumonia.

It is hard to determine when lung nodules become life-threatening cancer. But one indicator of a lung nodule's malignancy is its size.

At 2 milimeters or smaller, the risk of cancer is very small and remains so up to a nodule size of about 6-7 milimeters.

The risk of cancer becomes 9%-10% at about 8 to 10 milimeters. And at larger than 1 centimeter, the risk of cancer is about 15%.

The density of a lung nodule is also a vital indicator of malignancy.

There are two main categories of lung nodule density: solid and subsolid. Subsolid nodules are further divided into pure ground-glass (nonsolid) and part-solid nodules.

According to a 2026 review article published in the New England Journal of Medicine, subsolid nodules are less prevalent than solid nodules, but they have "a higher likelihood of being malignant."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

It is said that radiologists see lung nodules in about 30% of chest CT scans. But that number may be rising.

A Dutch study published in 2023 cited an increase in lung nodule detections from 38% of scans in 2008 to 50% in 2019. The same study said "the proportion of patients in whom significant new nodules (≥ 5 mm) were reported increased from 9% in 2010 to 17% in 2017."

However, this may also be a result of the development of better scanning technology in recent years and the use of artificial intelligence to spot tumors.

Bearing in mind that most lung nodules are benign, lung cancer does tend to start with a lesion or nodule. And lung cancer remains the most common type of cancer and the most common cause of cancer death in the world.

The World Health Organization's International Agency for Research on Cancer says that in 2024 almost 2.65 million people were diagnosed with lung cancer and more than 1.8 million people died from the disease.

The former Manchester United and England defender is now a YouTube and podcast star

Following his retirement as a player in 2011, it didn't take Gary Neville long to get the ball rolling on his next career, as he quickly became one of English football's most popular pundits.

After a decade of analysing the game for Sky Sports, the former Manchester United and England man diversified further, setting up The Overlap YouTube Channel in 2021.

This saw Neville shift his focus to in-depth conversations with some of the biggest names in sport, from Harry Kane and Anthony Joshua to Dina Asher-Smith. Over the past five years, the channel has become a huge success, with Neville admitting that its origins were more personal than commercial.

Neville insists that rather than spotting a gap in the market, it was his own desire to improve his own interviewing skills and move away from short-form, bite-sized social media content to something more meaningful that was his initial motivation.

“There was no gap in the market,” Neville tells FourFourTwo. “There was just a gap in my head of something that I was missing. It's a bit embarrassing to admit, but there’d be times at Sky when managers would come into the studio, there’d be Dave or Kelly, Carra and me, we’d ask them questions and I thought ‘I’m really bad at this’.

In a world where TikTok clips, YouTube Shorts and Instagram Reels often dominate the social media landscape, Neville did not want to follow the crowd.

“Lots of people were pushing me to do more bitesize content, 60 to 90 seconds, to fit TikTok and Instagram," he continues. "I didn’t want to do that, but I thought there was an opportunity to do two things – get better at interviewing people and keep traditional long-form interviews. So I just started walking with people. On a beach, on a golf course, and I just talked to them – a good conversation about football, boxing or whatever.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“It was never about podcasts. I don’t listen to podcasts, it was about becoming a better interviewer and creating an interesting television programme. That’s how I see it – it’s a television programme we put on YouTube.

"We do sometimes get described as a podcast, but to me it’s a visual thing. I’ve done podcasts where you do them remotely – you can be at home, the other people can be in their homes, and I don’t get it. I don’t feel it. I’ve got to be sat there with people to bounce off them, to feel their energy, to feel their enthusiasm.

“What has happened since then has been a great journey – it’s a team I love working with and I’m incredibly proud to be a part of. We never thought of it as a business, we just wanted to create something that people loved and would come back to watch every week.”

The team he mentions is led by co-founder Scott Melvin, who worked as a senior producer at Sky Sports on Super Sunday and Monday Night Football for 17 years, and is backed up by a staff with a background in television, working for Sky and BBC.

“It’s always a risk when you start something from scratch,” Melvin says. “We started the production company first, Buzz 16, then The Overlap grew out of that. What started off as a side hustle has become this thing we never expected it to be. We’ve all learned as we’ve gone along, but we didn’t start it as a business, it started off as Gary just having some fun on YouTube.

“Sky Bet came on board very early, were brilliant with us and are still a really important partner for us now. Then we started Stick to Football, which was the turning point. Again it was a bit of a punt because let’s be honest, it wasn’t a particularly revolutionary idea – let’s get five people around a table and talk about football. But the difference was the people.”

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

#1047. 125 years of Thomas Mann's 'Buddenbrooks'

This over 1,000-page masterpiece offers a panoramic view of society in the 19th century and exposes the collapse of a merchant family: unrecognized sons, disillusioned daughters and the loss of middle-class ideals.

Who would have imagined it in the beginning? A 26-year-old man without a high school diploma, but greatly ambitious, writes a two-pound book with a melancholy undertone. "I'm not exactly delighted," his publisher initially responded. But he ended up publishing the novel anyway, more out of goodwill than conviction. And the rest is history.

For many, Thomas Mann's Buddenbrooks is considered THE German social novel. It is indeed a classic, and one that garnered the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929. Global fame, an international best-seller, and required reading for many German students. Anyone who mentions Thomas Mann thinks of Buddenbrooks in the same breath. Why is that?

Does the explanation lie in the autobiographical connections between the work and the author?

Thomas Mann was born in Lübeck to a merchant family, but his artistic aspirations did not fit in well in the middle-class mainstream. This struggle inspired Mann's first work. The inability of this sensitive bohemian to carry on the family's time-honored business after the death of his father was sniffed at and derided.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Reflecting the situation of his novel's character Hanno, Mann had a privileged life in a wealthy family, but one that was at risk of collapse. The aspiring novelist also had to withstand disappointing the expectations of others. He was forced to defend his dream of an artistic life. Yet as much as he was inspired by real life, he forcefully altered these biographical details to place his unique literary mark on his writing.

But does that really matter in light of people who choose not to make the distinction between an author's life and his work? Even though the name "Lübeck" does not appear in the novel, citizens there felt markedly insulted after the publication of Buddenbrooks in 1901.

That likely lies in the fact that the image the author portrayed was not one of an idyllic northern German city, but one of a place that had difficulty blending tradition with modernity.

This contradiction is also seen in each of the figures in the novel. Nothing is like it appears. Mann lays down this foundation of this skepticism from the very beginning, in a scene taking place on a very ordinary Thursday in October 1835. The Buddenbrook family comes together for their ordinary late lunch.

"There they all sat, on heavy, high-backed chairs, consuming good heavy food from good silver plates, drinking full-bodied wines and expressing their views freely on all subjects. When they began to talk shop, they slipped unconsciously more and more into dialect, and used the clumsy but comfortable idioms that seemed to embody to them the business efficiency and the easy well-being of their community. Sometimes they even used an over-drawn pronunciation by way of making fun of themselves and each other, and relished their clipped phrases and exaggerated vowels with the same heartiness they did their food."

There sits the leader of the family company, Johann Buddenbrook the Elder, and his wife, his son and counsel Jean, along with his family. The grandchildren are also there: Tony the dreamer, the quarrelsome rebel Christian, and Thomas, the eldest grandchild.

It is Thomas who is supposed to later take on the responsibility of continuing the family tradition, regardless of the cost. Mann weaves his narrative work starting with this main family, and then across several generations.

But appearances in the family are deceptive. The reader senses it's all headed toward a downfall. The new house is taken over from a family that was once as illustrious as the Buddenbrooks, but faced financial ruin and had to leave.

Johann and his family aim to make a better go of it. They make decisions on what is demanded economically, but fail — financially, interpersonally, and mentally.

Tony and Thomas end up falling in love with people not befitting their social standing, but do not have the courage to stand up to their parents. They enter marriages of convenience, yet it is these partnerships that paradoxically set disaster in motion.

From an early age, Thomas Mann was influenced by Schopenhauer's pessimistic notion of the will being a blind force at work in the world. Thus, there is likewise no escape for the Buddenbrooks. They speak of emotions and morality, yet it is money and economics that steer the ship. Failure, decline and even death seem to be the only viable outcome.

Mann also punctuates this hopelessness in a stylistic manner, by consistently repeating entire passages word for word, or evoking motifs such as the family registry or the estate in all their various forms.

The extent of this demise appears linguistically molded and exaggerated. The Buddenbrooks, this proud north German family of refinement, actually speaks the vernacular studded with empty French expressions. "Je, den Düwel ook, c'est la question, ma très chère demoiselle!"

The lowly servants, the courtesans, and the demi-monde: all of them speak the language of the street, raw and unpolished. In a virtuoso manner, Thomas Mann orchestrated this mass of voices into a panorama of society in the 19th century. The snobbishness on the part of the Buddenbrooks thus appears as a relic of a long lost time. It's a symbol of their inability to adapt to change and place their faith in progress.

Yet the fact that this extensive work spanning several generations does not get weighed down by aesthetic excess is purely due to Mann's brilliance as an author. He is able to bring every one of his numerous characters to life in words. Life that is full of complexity, contradictions and ambiguities. Some of these characters accompany the reader page for page; others appear only briefly.

And yet one begins to contemplate how someone like Grünlich could become a dodgy, unscrupulous husband and catches oneself wanting to chase the fearful Hanno out of the music conservatory and yell to him: "Go, throw yourself into life! You are not a failure." It is precisely this empathy that spurs one on to read through the night and prompts one to chuckle at all the intricate sentences and philosophical digressions.

Thomas Mann: Buddenbrooks, Vintage Classics / Penguin Random House, (German title: Buddenbrooks, 1901). English translation: John E. Woods

Thomas Mann was born into a privileged Lübeck merchant family in 1875. He died in Zurich, Switzerland in 1955. "I am a townsman, a citizen, a child and a great-grandchild of German bourgeois society," the author once wrote about himself. Mann received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929 for his debut novel, Buddenbrooks. He also garnered numerous other prizes and honors for his extensive work, including Death in Venice (1911), The Magic Mountain (1924), and the tetralogy Joseph and His Brothers (1933-1943). He emigrated to Switzerland in 1933, and to the US in 1938. From there, he made his famous radio commentaries in which he agitated against the Nazis. He returned to Switzerland in 1952.

This article was first published as part of the series 100 German must-reads.

Martinez was sent off against Chelsea on the weekend after a string of errors in recent games

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Michael Carrick has insisted he does not doubt Lisandro Martinez’s commitment to Manchester United – even after the defender launched a verbal attack on sporting director Jason Wilcox and was then sent off in Saturday’s defeat to Chelsea.

The Argentinian, who apologised after criticising Wilcox and United’s recruitment following the loss to Atletico Madrid, has been at fault for a series of goals in recent weeks and his red card at Stamford Bridge condemned Carrick’s team to a third consecutive setback.

Martinez elbowed Chelsea defender Wesley Fofana to concede a penalty, which Cole Palmer scored, and collect his second yellow card, meaning he will be suspended for Sunday’s game against Aston Villa.

The Argentina international is out of contract in the summer, though United have the option to extend his deal for a further year.

But Carrick was adamant he was not questioning the defender’s attitude, saying: “I've got no concerns about commitment at all. Things happen in football. Sometimes you do things, sometimes you make a decision, sometimes you make mistakes, sometimes goes well for you. But the commitment is not an issue for sure.”

Captain Bruno Fernandes has also given an explosive post-match interview recently, criticising Carrick’s tactics after the 4-1 loss to Como.

But Carrick said he is not worried about the image that his squad lack discipline, adding: “The dressing room is a good, good place, so perceptions are a funny thing. They can they can they can make things look all sorts of different ways and think about all sorts of different things. The commitment of the players to the club, to me, to each other – I don't question that at all. We need to play better, we can make better decisions, but commitment's not a thing at all.”

United face Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday with the under-pressure Carrick claiming he can’t wait for the match.

“You might think I'm crazy with the results we've had and what's going on, but I'm genuinely, really can't wait for the game,” he said.

United will again be without Patrick Dorgu and Luke Shaw. The England left-back will be out until the international break but the Denmark international is back in training, though he will not be involved against Roma.

Carrick is waiting to see when forward Marcus Rashford is fit to return. “We'll just have to see day by day how he keeps improving,” he added.

The former Arsenal and Manchester United rivals are now pals off the pitch

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As players, Ian Wright and Roy Keane spent much of their careers on opposite sides of one of English football’s fiercest rivalries.

The Arsenal great and former Manchester United captain both possessed the competitive spirit that meant exchanging pleasantries and forging friendships was never high on their to-do list when league titles were on the line.

Football, though, has that habit of bringing together different characters and the pair have now developed a genuine bond away from the pitch. This is clear to anyone who watches The Overlap, where the two rivals have had a chance to show off a different side to their personalities.

““I remember when Gary first got in touch and said who he was going to get involved,” Wright tells FourFourTwo when asked about how his link-up with Gary Neville on The Overlap came about.

“I said ‘If you could get that crew together, that’d be brilliant’. We met up, and when we spoke, it just felt natural. The way we speak on camera is the way we are with each other off camera, too.

"I’m with people I genuinely like, and we’ve got a friendship and a bond now that is real. Nobody is afraid to pull anyone else up if they get something wrong or say something we don’t agree with, but it’s everyone’s love for the game that really comes across.”

During Wright and Keane's pomp in the 1990s, Arsenal and Manchester United's title battles set up a number of era-defining bitter Premier League clashes, making it hard for anyone to believe that two of the main protagonists would end up as such good friends.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“Mine and Roy’s relationship on the pitch was fractious,” Wright admits. “If I came in his vicinity, it was never going to be nice.

“But that was because of the teams we were playing for and what was expected of us, especially trying to deal with that Man United side. It was so dominant and so great.

"If you’d said to me back then that we would be friends now, would I have believed it? No, never. I never would have thought we’d be this close."

However, as the duo embarked on successful media careers, they soon found that they were kindred spirits.

“But it started when we were both doing punditry," former England man Wright adds. "We met up a few times and it was just fine, because people don’t understand Roy, he’s not an ogre! He’s not some guy that’s just in your face.

"He’ll respect you if you’re respectful, you’d never go into a studio with Roy and find he’d be rude or disrespectful. I love the fact you never know what he might say.”

The water cycle is global, yet its accounting is not. Rain, rivers and underground water cross borders freely, but water use is reported by country. The budget for the world’s total usage is therefore only as reliable as the weakest report. When a country cannot measure usage, its water is lost from global accounting — and with it, any claim to a fair share.

#1042. Uefa still waiting on answers from Fifa over Gianni Infantino controversies as deadline looms

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Uefa have demanded answers over a number of controversies at Fifa during Infantino’s presidency

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Uefa is still awaiting answers to a wide-ranging series of inquiries submitted to Fifa regarding Gianni Infantino’s presidency, with the deadline for a reply fast approaching.

On 19 October, Uefa general secretary Theodore Theodoridis formally wrote to his Fifa counterpart Mattias Grafstrom, outlining 42 specific topics requiring clarification on behalf of European members serving on the Fifa Council.

The request sought transparency over Infantino’s now-shelved proposal to secure private investment for a company to handle the World Cup’s commercial operations. It also asked for the disclosure of documentation concerning the Folarin Balogun disciplinary case, alongside guarantees and explanations regarding potential conflicts of interest. The letter requested substantive responses by 2 November.

It is understood that as of midday Central European Time on Monday, no such response had been received.

The communication followed a Fifa Council session on 15 October, during which Infantino was directly questioned by members. Football Association chair and Fifa vice-president Debbie Hewitt subsequently noted that representatives had been instructed to submit their remaining queries in writing.

The letter from Theodoridis brought together the collective concerns of the European Council members into a single document.

"These questions require answers now," he wrote.

"They cannot be deferred until the next meeting of the Fifa Council – nor can future governance reforms substitute for scrutiny of decisions already taken and accountability for them."

In response to an initial query regarding the correspondence on 20 October, a Fifa spokesperson said: "The Fifa governance regulations state that Council meetings and their associated documentation are confidential.

"While Fifa intends to reply to questions submitted by its Council members it has no intention of breaching confidentiality by commenting on internal communication and/or documentation to media.

"Fifa considers respect for these regulations to be a function of respect for the Council itself and for its individual members. Fifa will always maintain this respect and will not be drawn into any exchange with any third parties that undermines this."

Fifa was approached for fresh comment on Monday.

The Fifa Council is not scheduled to gather again until 16 December. Uefa has committed to identifying a credible alternative candidate to challenge Infantino in the Fifa presidential election next March.

The deadline for submitting candidacies is 18 November.

A Leeds United fan who suffered a medical emergency before October’s meeting with Manchester United has died, the club has confirmed.

Colin Westby, 68, was taken to hospital by ambulance after requiring medical attention around half an hour before kick-off at Elland Road on 18 October. He was then placed in a medically-induced coma.

Leeds initially praised the “rapid action” of stewards and medical staff on the day, and say they are “heartbroken” to learn the news of his passing.

“Leeds United are heartbroken to learn of the passing of supporter Colin Westby at the age of 68,” a club statement read.

“Colin suffered a medical emergency ahead of our Premier League fixture with Manchester United on Sunday 18 October at Elland Road.

“After being transferred to hospital, he was placed into a medically induced coma and sadly following a period of unresponsiveness, the decision was made to withdraw life support.”

Westby was a season ticket holder at Leeds for 50 years and will be honoured during Leeds’ next Premier League fixture this weekend.

“The thoughts of everyone at Leeds United are with Colin’s family and friends at this sad time,” the statement continued.

“We will pay tribute to Colin in the 68th minute of our next Premier League fixture with Tottenham Hotspur, on Saturday 7 November.”

Marching Out Together, the official fan group for Leeds’ LGBTQ+ fans, also paid tribute to a “friend of our MOuT family” on social media.

“We were so sorry to hear of the passing of Colin Westby, a Leeds fan for 50+ years and friend of our MOuT family,” a statement read.

“Love and light to all who were with him that day, and above all to his family and friends.

“Please recognise Colin in the 68th minute on Saturday.”

#1039. Arsenal nous frustrates Liverpool as 14-year Anfield hoodoo ends with statement win

It is clear and obvious that Arsenal will be the team to beat in the Premier League title race, especially given that we do not yet know the fate of faltering Manchester City and their looming punishment.

A statement victory against Liverpool, their first in the league at Anfield since 2012, took Arsenal back to the top. And who would bet against them staying there and retaining their title?

Few would when they defend and manage a game – and it was game management in every sense – like this. From the formidable to the cynical – that was the statement. Against the Scousers, Arsenal had the nous.

“The mission was something we didn’t complete in 14 years,” Mikel Arteta said, having famously – in an Amazon documentary series – played You’ll Never Walk Alone to his players as they walked out to train to try and overcome a perceived mental block.

“There are reasons for that. Some of it psychological, some of it moments we did not nail on the pitch,” the Arsenal manager added of the winless run.

The result means that the north Londoners have already now won away at Villa Park, the Stadium of Light, the City Ground and Anfield. Stadiums where they dropped points last season. And that feels ominous.

A win would maybe have thrust Liverpool into the title race. Instead, under Andoni Iraola, and with an evolving young team – with promising 19-year-old midfielder Trey Nyoni handed his league debut – they are already nine points behind after just nine matches.

It is also clear, however, that they could have prevented this defeat having somehow been denied a first-half penalty after Alexander Isak’s shirt was blatantly pulled by Jurrien Timber as the striker tried to head home a cross.

Referee Andy Madley may have missed it, but what was the excuse of Stuart Attwell, the VAR? It was a stunningly poor decision – another bad day for Pro Ref and the use of technology.

It might be argued that Timber did not pull hard enough to prevent Isak from reaching the ball. But the defender grabbed the shirt and continued to hold it for a long time. It had to be a penalty. Little wonder Iraola said Isak should dive next time. Who can blame him?

What is also clear and obvious is that, once again, Arsenal’s resilience, defensive determination and appetite for toughing it out will be their greatest weapons. They are certainly, under Arteta, not here to win friends – just to win matches and trophies.

“That defensive line, that togetherness we have is undefeated. It’s something I have never seen before,” Declan Rice, who was also a stand-out performer and delivered a fine assist for the winner, said.

Arsenal’s version of the Yellow Wall was, indeed, hugely impressive – it is now six clean sheets from their nine league games and, despite all their pressure, Liverpool did not have a shot on target. That has never happened in the Premier League since such statistics started to be compiled in 2003 (422 games ago).

“That’s incredible. It did not feel like it on the pitch. Again, it’s the commitment of every single player,” Arteta said. And that was indisputable.

Even the expected second-half momentum, the expected surge of attack after attack as Liverpool faced the Kop, crashed on Arsenal’s back line. The visitors were so well-drilled that they stifled space – they refused to crumble.

Arsenal put their bodies on the line with blocks and tackles and a bit of time-wasting. There were dark arts, especially from both centre-halves with Gabriel going unpunished after claiming he was struck in the face by Isak early on – VAR anyone? – and the otherwise outstanding Ezri Konsa throwing himself to the ground after minimal contact from the Liverpool centre-forward.

In fairness there was also a bit of that from an increasingly frustrated Liverpool with Alexis Mac Allister going down after touching heads with Noni Madueke, having already tried to provoke Martin Odegaard with a hand to the head when the Arsenal captain was on the turf. That was not good from Mac Allister either.

And the only goal? Again, more frustration for Liverpool. It was well-constructed from Arsenal, but only after Alisson Becker’s loose goal kick, aimed towards Jérémy Jacquet, who was slow to react, was intercepted by Odegaard with Bruno Guimarães poking the ball to the right, where it was collected by Madueke.

There was an overlap by Rice and his low centre was precise and dangerous across the face of the six-yard area, with Virgil van Dijk unsure what to do. It ran beyond the far post where Kai Havertz side-footed home.

"Absolutely brilliant from Arsenal." Kai Havertz gives Arsenal an early lead at Anfield! ⚡️ https://t.co/eeyhRcLlel

After that? Liverpool swarmed over Arsenal, particularly in the first-half with Florian Wirtz’s free-kick cannoning back off the crossbar and Mac Allister somehow heading over. He was six yards out and unmarked, it was a glorious chance.

That was the hosts’ last tangible opportunity to score. As well as Arsenal defended, it was not a good afternoon for Liverpool’s forwards, Bradley Barcola in particular, although it was interesting to see Arsenal double-up on Rio Ngumoha when he came on. Arteta reacted by bringing on a second left-back, in Piero Hincapié.

Arsenal had the best chance with Alisson denying Christos Tzolis as the Greek winger’s low volley threatened to arc around him.

For Liverpool it became frantic. They could not surf the emotion, not against this battle-hardened Arsenal.

Boos rang out at the end – signs of how Arsenal had frustrated Liverpool – as Arteta gained his first win at Anfield as a manager. He was in the last Arsenal team to win here as a player 14 years ago. But this one meant more – that was also clear and obvious as he joyfully jumped into the arms of his assistant, Gabriel Heinze.

Pride? No disappointment. Disappointment. We played at home. We had some opportunities. Obviously we tried everything. We could have done better in the last 15 minutes to get balls in the box but it wasn’t enough. That’s why it’s a disappointment.

After we conceded we started to play much better. We created the big chance for Alexis which could have changed the game. It didn’t happen. We kept pushing and pushing.

I think there was also a clear penalty. I have seen it back. I’ve seen it being given on other occasions. [Should Alex have made more of it. Maybe the VAR doesn’t notice it…] The VAR doesn’t notice it? We have 50 cameras, even more. Why do you have to complain more if they have 50 cameras. They spotted it because everyone’s seen it. It wasn’t given, we lose the game. Congratulations to Arsenal.

When someone new comes in the building it just takes a bit if time. Our fans can see there is so much improvement and we work out socks off. What we do need as well is results.

Havertz: “It means a lot to the whole football club. It is important. It’s what they deserve [the fans]. We all know what this stadium is about. We knew it was coming but we all stuck together, defended together. Ninety per cent of the goal belongs to that man [Rice].”

Rice: “That’s the Anfield way. That is what Liverpool do. This stadium creates waves and waves of attacks. Relentless. That defensive line, that togetherness we have is undefeated. It’s something I’ve never seen before. The manager had an honest conversation with me and said I could do even more for this club [in terms of assists and goals]. It’s always tiring coming here. First win in 14 years and my first win here too. It’s demanding. An amazing result. I have learnt that you can only take the table seriously in February and March and all you can do until then is win as many as you can.”

Barcola’s last-gasp cross is blocked and that is that.

Isak is caught in the offside trap when chasing Barcola’s hook over the top that could have put him through one-on-one.

Barcola cannot impart any power on a shot from eight yards after he pounced following some pinball passes and ricochets. Raya easily stops it. A shot on target.

Munoz, sandwiched between Hincapie and Calafiori, manages to get his head on Koumas’s flick on at the back post bit cannot get any power on it.

Ngumoha’s shot is deflected behind for a corner.

Van Dijk is playing as a centre-forward now but Gyojkeres’ lack of pace ruins Arsenal’s chances of exploiting his absence at the back from a counter-attack when he can’t get to Lewis-Skelly’s upfield pass.

Calafiori blocks Ngumoha’s left-foot shot out for a throw-in.

Calafiori shins a pass into touch when under pressure from Ngumoha. Still no Liverpool shot on target.

Hincapié goes to left-back with Calafiori in front of him.

Koumas → AraujoMuñoz  → WirtzTsimikas → Kerkez

Mac Allister goes down clutching his head after winding up Arsenal with a slap on Odegaard. Madueke had narrowed the gap and touched Mac Allister’s forehead with his own but sanity prevails and Madueke is not sanctioned. Mac Allister and Timber are booked.

Liverpool keep huffing and puffing around the Arsenal box but the champions seem more and more convinced that their house is made of bricks.

You will go a long way this season before you see a better save than the one Alisson Becker has just produced to keep Liverpool in the contest. The speed and the reflexes to get down and turn Tzolis’s shot around the corner was breathtaking. A reminder, if it were needed, of what an impossible job Liverpool will have to replace him one day.

Van Dijk leathers a shot from 25 yards that loops up over to the right. Ngumoha chases it and keeps it in, working it back to MacAllister whose cross is plucked out of the air by Raya.

Superb save from Alisson low to his left to turn Tzolis’s blistering daisy-cutter round the post.

A brilliant save from Alisson to deny Tzolis! 🧤 https://t.co/0K2DPuUMEu

“It’s a joke, an absolute joke,” says Gary Neville about the protocol that kept Kerkez out of the game for a minute when hurt accidentally.

Van Dijk cuts out Tzolis’s pass from the left intended for Calafiori on an underlapping run into the box.

Liverpool defend the corner though at the price of going down to 10 because Kerkez went down after a collision of heads.

Tzolis wastes a golden opportunity on the break by opting not to shoot as Alisson came out to meet him but centre it for Odegaard instead. Jacquet put his foot in to divert it over the bar.

Barcola goes skipping down the left and manages to slide a pass through Timber’s legs for Wirtz, who has to stretch to control it, pirouettes and then wastes it 16 yards out, dead centre, by striking it into a defender. Kerkez stops a possible counter-attack with a foul on Madueke that puts him in the book.

Raya gives the ball away cheaply but the bounce is awkward for Barcola whose attempt to head it on for Isak is too loopy and gives the keeper the time to rush out and regather.

Arsenal waste a few seconds after Van Dijk was penalised for a foul on Bruno. They decide to take him off but even when the substitution is completed, they still dawdle over the restart.

Mac Allister, in shooting territory 25 yards out, tries to fizz a pass to Wirtz in the box instead and Arsenal scramble it away.

Both players receive rousing receptions on departure and entry.

The more you watch Jéremy Jacquet, the easier it is to understand why Liverpool made the decision to not follow up interest in Marc Guehi back in January. The young Frenchman has been – to borrow a phrase from his national team manager Zinedine Zidane – “very good; very, very good” since he was thrust into the team and he’s shown it again in this match.

Liverpool take the free-kick quickly and Kerkez releases Isak down the left to lash a left-foot shot over the angle of left post and crossbar.

Madueke is booked for legging up Barcola who threatened to race away on a counter after Van Dijk had blocked Bruno’s shot.

Arsenal hold their nerve and their lines when Wirtz, Nyoni and Gakpo try to thread passes in to feet in the penalty area, managing to make the blocks as Liverpool keep probing.

There’s a groan when Gakpo’s cross from the right hits Bruno. Then Isak was caught offside when turning the ball around the corner for Wirtz to have a shot.

Arsenal set up solidly in defensive lines to stop Liverpool raising the tempo on which they thrived in the first half.

Araujo wends his way around Calafiori after good work from Isak and crosses towards the penalty spot. Gabriel hooks the ball away with Wirtz and Isak on their heels around the 18-yard line.

Victor Muñoz has gone through a rigorous half-time warm up, which indicates he won’t be far away from getting minutes. Liverpool aren’t out of this, by any means, but they need a step up again.

Liverpool re-start “kicking into the Kop” in the words of Ian Wright. A ling chip down the right gives Gakpo something to chase but he can’t get round Calafiori who shepherds it out for a goal-kick.

Liverpool will be pleased with their response to going behind but very frustrated also at not, at least, being level. Arsenal started superbly and got their goal but Liverpool have swarmed all over them since. It has been a bit too frantic at times. There have been a series of penalty appeals, most of which were rightly ignored. But Arsenal got away with one when Jurrien Timber clearly pulled at Alexander Isak’s shirt, preventing him from heading a cross. It is the kind of incident that really makes you wonder what the VAR is doing.

Arsenal have been on the ropes since opening the scoring as wave after wave of Liverpool attacks swarm towards their box. But so far they retain their lead but will have to adjust their midfield and forward lines soon as it’s been boy stood on the burning deck stuff from Rice at times. Mac Allister, who has become a beast in the air recently, should have equalised but seemed to stoop into it and get under it rather than heading it down.

Barcola is booked for catching Timber in a sliding tackle and his visible contempt for the decision means there will be no reprieve.

With two minutes of stoppage time signalled Arsenal are on a rare attack but Tozolis again doesn’t release the ball when he should and slows it down.

Liverpool seem intent on trying to score a perfect goal. The irony is that it’s old fashioned pace and being direct that is starting to unsettle Arsenal. Bradley Barcola, therefore, needs to step up. He’s been on the edges so far and it’s crying out for him to have a persistent run at Jurrien Timber and ask him some big questions.

Mac Allister misses a sitter. He eluded his midfield marker and met Kerkez’s perfect cross between the penalty spot and six-yard line but steered it over. Now it’s Calafiori’s turn to upbraid the players ahead of him.

Rice is becoming very annoyed about a lack of support from his front players in providing a viable outlet when he wins the ball. He is waving his arms and chuntering away.

Wirtz takes the free-kick bending it with dip and whip over Raya but into the heart of the crossbar. Arsenal butcher their counter-attacking opportunity.

Timber is penalised for a decent-looking tackle on Isak just outside the box on the Liverpool left. That comes a moment after the referee gave Liverpool a corner despite Mac Allister’s cross not touching an Arsenal player. They are going spare and one can sympathise with them.

There’s no room at all in the Arsenal penalty area as first Mac Allister tries to fizz a pass through the massed ranks then Isak weaves an opening for a left-foot shot that he smacks into the hoardings, 3ft wide and rising.

Arsenal enjoy a moment of respite on a rapid counter down the right but Bruno takes too many touches when found by Odegaard in the middle, 18 yards out, allowing Mac Allister to tie him up.

Sky digs out a replay from the 21st minute which clearly shows Timber with a fistful of Isak’s shirt that stopped him reaching a cross. But he, unlike the bench, did not appeal for a penalty. “He is nice,” says Gary Neville disdainfully.

Kerkez cushions a pass on his thigh when he ghosts into the centre-forward position and then tamely lobs a volley wide from 18 yards. Liverpool are swarming the Arsenal penalty area.

Liverpool are laying siege at the moment, snapping into tackles, putting in crosses, taking one too many touches to surprise Arsenal. Now Gakpo goes down in the box when confronted by Tzolis who does make contact but not enough for Madley or the VAR after a look.

Liverpool corner from the right. Van Dijk wins the header and Isak, creeping round Konsa, is there to tap it in, but Raya is alert and pushes it behind before Isak can pounce.

Tzoli’s cross from the left is met at the back post by Timber who tries to knock it back across the six-yard box to Havertz but Timber gets in the way.

Mac Allister’s crossfield pearler picks out Kerkez but he hits the first defender with his cross and Arsenal counter at pace and Madueke faces Kerkez up but dawdles instead of trying to dribble past him. He waits for reinforcements and then cuts it back to Bruno who bends a pass through the six-yard box from the right of the D that Tzolis slides in but just cannot reach

The Arsenal goal has been a real tonic for Liverpool who are now hounding Arsenal’s players when in possession and gorging on mistakes, roared on by a raucous crowd. The volume is as high as I’ve heard for ages.

Two close shaves for Arsenal immediately after the goal, Rice needing to get back to stop Konsa’s mistake giving Wirtz a path to goal and then Barcola fades a cross/shot from the left of the D just beyond the right post.

Liverpool 0 Arsenal 1 (Havertz) Odegaard who, with Rice and Bruno, have dominated midfield, triggers the press when Liverpool play out from the back, disrupting a pass then running back to collect his interception. He strolls forward and plays it to Madueke who waits for Rice’s run on the overlap. The England midfielder delivers perfectly from the right and Havertz is Johnny on the spot at the back post to crash a shot past the scrambling Alisson.

"Absolutely brilliant from Arsenal." Kai Havertz gives Arsenal an early lead at Anfield! ⚡️ https://t.co/eeyhRcLlel

Van Dijk semi-deliberately collides with Havertz after clearing the ball very forcefully.

Arsenal have come with one intention in mind, seemingly, and that is to spoil the game. Already in the opening 14 minutes we have seen Gabriel go down as if he had been cracked on the chin by Tyson Fury and now Kai Havertz has reacted bizarrely to a straightforward coming together with Virgil van Dijk. They are better than that, as they have just shown with Havertz’s opening goal, and Liverpool will have to be cute if they are to find a way back into the contest.

Odegaard pushes up behind Tzolis and frees the winger for a run into the box. Araujo stalsk him stride for stride and uses his strength to lever him off the ball which rolls out for a goal-kick.

Arsenal are dominating possession but when they go back to Raya he makes a rare error with his feet and launches a 50-yard pass over Madueke’s head into touch.

Nyoni gets away without a card after another foul, this one on Havertz when Nyoni’s touch let him down and he booted the Arsenal forward. Mikel Arteta is rightly peeved that the referee has let him off again. Youth buys you leeway with Andy Madley.

Liverpool counter at pace down the middle but Raya is very sharply off his line to deal with the long pass. That’s the source of all the jargon about ‘verticality’ both managers inflicted on us in the build-up.

Arsenal corner after Tzolis was given space to run into down the left but hit Jacquet with his square pass when he made the 18-yard line. Arsenal take it short and seem to catch Tzolis by surprise and he is quickly closed down before he can give it precisely back to Rice.

Liverpool work the ball up the left to Kerkez who pings it infield to Isak. he opens his body to spay it into the stride of Gakpo who drags a right-foot shot wide of the left post.

Kerkez knocks the ball out for an Arsenal throw but immediately gets one back for his side when Van Dijk bullies Havertz who was trying to shield it.

Gabriel milks the life out of a tussle with Gakpo, going down clutching his face when slapped on the chest. A great defender but a ridiculous human being.

Arsenal kick off attacking the Kop but do not retain possession from Odegaard’s forward pass and there’s some counter-thrust until Timber takes possession on the right and drives forward to give it to Odegaard who is clumsily fouled by Nyoni who catches his ankle with his studs. Would have been a yellow for anyone else, I’d say, and the timing also made the referee reluctant.

This is a big day for Andoni Iraola and his emerging team and it feels like the stadium has its mojo back. It’s colourfully, lively and noisy and You’ll Never Walk Alone is being sung as loudly at any point since Liverpool were crowned champions in the spring of 2025. There is a feeling amongst home supporters that they fancy this today: that, in itself, shows progress because it wasn’t the case when Nottingham Forest and Fulham were the first Premier League visitors this season.

Any problems, he says, “let’s have a sensible chat” and he reminds them that they are responsible for their teams’ conduct as the strains of You’ll Never Walk Alone die down.

And now wreaths are laid in memory of the fallen followed by the Last Post.

Liverpool in Ron Yeatsian all red, Arsenal in that hideous faded yellow and blue. The yellow on Arsenal away kits should always be bright primrose. She didn’t wear a mustard ribbon did she, in the merry month of May?

Trey Nyoni is only the second ever teenager to make his first league start for Liverpool against the reigning English champions, after Raheem Sterling v Man City in August 2012. #LFC

The Arsenal players have long completed their warm-up and returned to the changing rooms. Liverpool have stayed out on the pitch and have just been involved in a lengthy team huddle with Virgil van Dijk conducting his own team talk in front of the Kop before they disperse and head back down the tunnel.

"He's brought a spirit that Liverpool really lacked last season" Jamie Carragher on the Liverpool fans taking to Ronald Araújo 🤝 https://t.co/dleLirsm2v

It’s not about me [being brave in picking Nyoni], it’s about Trey. In training he has shown he has the level. For us he’s very good without the ball. It’s a big challenge for him but [he is ready].

He is young but covers a lot of space. He is aggressive as well without the ball, calm in possession, good communicating with his team-mates which is good when you know how Arsenal play. You need a lot of change of marks [positions]. There have to be a lot of things done there in the middle and he has done that in other games.

The aggression we had [against Brighton, never resting] in their structures, we go again, recover, go vertical, attack the spaces in behind, win the chance battle, one v one situations. Don’t concede territory against teams like Brighton and Arsenal. We have to be as aggressive as we were in that match.

Teams like this don’t give you easy situations [to score]. We have to be good in one v one, shots from outside the box, finishes, set plays – we should be a team that is strong in set plays. You won’t get many chances against Arsenal and when you have one you’ve got to grab it.

Yes we had good results with Bournemouth against Arsenal but the strengths of my team in Liverpool are different so you have to approach it in a different way. There are things I can use [from Bournemouth] but not a lot.

Arsenal have lost three of their last four games against Bournemouth when Iraola was in charge.

We have been very close [to winning at Anfield in the last four seasons] but moments have decided those games. We have to be really precise in those moments for victory here and that has to be the case today.

Every manager has different solutions and a different approach and Andoni’s is very clear. We expect a different game to that one [last year when Arne Slot’s side won 1-0]. It is a team that is very vertical with a real capacity to create chaos from almost all situations. They’re very good in the high press with great individuals.

[On selection] We have had issues this week with ankles and other things and had to be smart how we manage the minutes today to have players for the minutes they are available for. The conditions and the context force you to make certain decisions [on Tzolis coming straight back in after a month out].

We can’t wait. This is the kind of opportunity, challenge, mission you want to come to Anfield for.

There will be a commemoration of the fallen and pledge to care for the living before the match.
